lead: Every circuit is a set of elements joined by ideal wires. The three passive elements are the resistor R, the inductor L and the capacitor C, and each is defined by one rule that ties the voltage v across it to the current i through it. The resistor turns electrical energy into heat; the inductor and the capacitor store energy and give it back later. Every later method in the subject is built on these three rules.

blocks.text: Charge q is measured in coulombs (C). Current is the rate at which charge flows past a point: i = dq/dt, in amperes (A), where 1 A = 1 C/s. Voltage between two points is the energy needed to move one coulomb of charge from one point to the other: v = dw/dq, in volts (V), where 1 V = 1 J/C.

Power is the rate of energy flow: p = dw/dt = (dw/dq)(dq/dt) = v·i, in watts (W). Use the passive sign convention: draw the current reference arrow so that it enters the + terminal of the element. Then p = vi is the power the element absorbs. A negative p means the element is delivering power, which is what a source normally does.

A DC quantity is constant in time (a 12 V car battery); an AC quantity changes with time, usually as a sinusoid (the 230 V, 50 Hz wall socket). The element laws below hold at every instant, so they serve both.

Resistance R is the opposition to current that turns electrical energy into heat. For a uniform wire of resistivity ρ, length l and area A, R = ρl/A. Inductance L is the flux linkage per ampere of a coil, L = Nφ/i, where N is the number of turns and φ the flux in webers. Capacitance C is the charge stored per volt, C = q/v; for two parallel plates of area A, gap d and permittivity ε, C = εA/d.

G = 1/R is the conductance in siemens (S); the integrals run from t₀ to t. Units follow from the laws: 1 Ω = 1 V/A, 1 H = 1 V·s/A, 1 F = 1 A·s/V. Use the integral form when the other quantity is known, and add the starting value i(t₀) or v(t₀).

The energy formulas come from the power: for the inductor p = Li di/dt = d(½Li²)/dt, and for the capacitor p = Cv dv/dt = d(½Cv²)/dt. Ideal L and C only store energy and return it. All three elements are linear (R, L, C constant), passive (they cannot deliver more energy than they received) and bilateral (the law is the same with the terminals swapped).

sections.h3: What cannot jump, and real components

blocks.text: Because v = L di/dt, a sudden jump in inductor current would need an infinite voltage. So the current through an inductor is continuous: iL(0⁺) = iL(0⁻). In the same way the voltage across a capacitor is continuous: vC(0⁺) = vC(0⁻). The inductor's voltage and the capacitor's current can jump. These two facts give the initial conditions used later in transient analysis.

Real components are not ideal. Model a real inductor as an ideal L in series with its winding resistance R<sub>w</sub>, which dissipates i²R<sub>w</sub>. A real capacitor has leakage and an equivalent series resistance (ESR). A filament lamp, whose resistance rises as it heats, is not linear.

spec.aria: Three panels: a 12 ohm resistor with 2 A gives 24 V; a 0.5 H inductor with current rising at 40 A per second gives 20 V; a 100 microfarad capacitor with voltage rising at 200 V per second takes 20 mA. Energy stored: 1 J and 5 mJ.

examples.question: A 12 Ω resistor carries 2 A. A 0.5 H inductor carries 2 A with di/dt = 40 A/s. A 100 μF capacitor has 10 V across it with dv/dt = 200 V/s. Using the passive sign convention, find v<sub>R</sub>, v<sub>L</sub>, i<sub>C</sub>, the power absorbed by each element and the energy stored in L and C.
steps: Resistor: v<sub>R</sub> = Ri = 12 Ω × 2 A = 24 V. Power p<sub>R</sub> = i²R = (2 A)² × 12 Ω = 48 W, all turned into heat.
Inductor: v<sub>L</sub> = L di/dt = 0.5 H × 40 A/s = 20 V. Power p<sub>L</sub> = v<sub>L</sub>i = 20 V × 2 A = 40 W, flowing into the magnetic field.

Capacitor: convert first, 100 μF = 100 × 10⁻⁶ F = 10⁻⁴ F. Then i<sub>C</sub> = C dv/dt = 10⁻⁴ F × 200 V/s = 0.02 A = 20 mA. Power p<sub>C</sub> = 10 V × 0.02 A = 0.2 W, flowing into the electric field.
Stored energy: w<sub>L</sub> = ½Li² = ½ × 0.5 × 2² = 1 J; w<sub>C</sub> = ½Cv² = ½ × 10⁻⁴ × 10² = 0.005 J = 5 mJ.
Check: d(½Li²)/dt = Li di/dt = 0.5 × 2 × 40 = 40 W, the same as p<sub>L</sub>.
examples.answer: v<sub>R</sub> = 24 V, v<sub>L</sub> = 20 V, i<sub>C</sub> = 20 mA; powers 48 W, 40 W and 0.2 W absorbed; stored energies 1 J in L and 5 mJ in C.

examples.question: (a) An uncharged 20 μF capacitor is charged by a constant current of 10 mA for 20 ms, after which the current is zero. Find its voltage at 20 ms and at 1 s, and the energy stored. (b) A 0.2 H inductor carries 0 A at t = 0. A constant 6 V is applied across it for 0.1 s. Find the current at 0.1 s and the stored energy.
steps: Capacitor, integral form: v(t) = v(0) + (1/C)∫i dt. With v(0) = 0 and a constant current, the integral is i × t = 10 × 10⁻³ A × 20 × 10⁻³ s = 2 × 10⁻⁴ C.
After 20 ms the current is zero, so dv/dt = 0 and the ideal capacitor holds 10 V; at 1 s it still reads 10 V. Energy w = ½Cv² = ½ × 20 × 10⁻⁶ × 10² = 1 × 10⁻³ J = 1 mJ.
Inductor, integral form: i(t) = i(0) + (1/L)∫v dt = 0 + (6 V × 0.1 s)/0.2 H = 0.6/0.2 = 3 A.
examples.answer: (a) 10 V at 20 ms and still 10 V at 1 s, storing 1 mJ. (b) 3 A at 0.1 s, storing 0.9 J.

traps: Using v = iR for an inductor or a capacitor. Their laws are v = L di/dt and i = C dv/dt; a constant current gives zero inductor voltage, not iR.
Swapping the two derivative laws: the inductor's voltage depends on di/dt; the capacitor's current depends on dv/dt.
Saying that capacitor current cannot change suddenly. It is the capacitor voltage that is continuous; for the inductor it is the current.
Forgetting the prefix: 100 μF is 100 × 10⁻⁶ F, not 100 × 10⁻³ F; 50 mH is 50 × 10⁻³ H.
Calling ideal L and C lossy. They store and return energy; only resistance (including a coil's winding resistance) turns it into heat.

quiz.q: Define resistance, inductance and capacitance, with the unit of each.
quiz.a: Resistance is the opposition to current that turns electrical energy into heat, R = v/i, in ohms (Ω). Inductance is the flux linkage per ampere of a coil, L = Nφ/i, in henries (H). Capacitance is the charge stored per volt, C = q/v, in farads (F).

quiz.q: Why does an ideal inductor act as a short circuit, and an ideal capacitor as an open circuit, at DC steady state?
quiz.a: At DC steady state nothing changes, so di/dt = 0 and dv/dt = 0. Then v<sub>L</sub> = L di/dt = 0 for any current (a short circuit) and i<sub>C</sub> = C dv/dt = 0 for any voltage (an open circuit).

quiz.q: A 2 kΩ resistor carries 5 mA. Find its voltage and the power it absorbs.
A 0.2 H inductor has its current rising at 100 A/s while carrying 3 A. Find v<sub>L</sub> and the energy stored at that instant.
quiz.a: v<sub>L</sub> = L di/dt = 0.2 × 100 = 20 V. w = ½Li² = ½ × 0.2 × 3² = 0.9 J.

quiz.q: A 100 μF capacitor has v = 10 V and dv/dt = −50 V/s. Find i<sub>C</sub> and decide whether the capacitor is absorbing or delivering power.
quiz.a: i<sub>C</sub> = C dv/dt = 10⁻⁴ × (−50) = −5 mA. The minus sign means the real current flows against the reference arrow, out of the + terminal. Power p = vi = 10 × (−0.005) = −0.05 W: the capacitor is discharging and delivering 50 mW to the circuit.

quiz.q: A real coil of 0.4 H has winding resistance 5 Ω and carries a steady 2 A DC. Find its terminal voltage and the power it wastes.
quiz.a: At DC di/dt = 0, so the ideal L part drops 0 V. The winding resistance drops 2 A × 5 Ω = 10 V, so the terminal voltage is 10 V. It wastes i²R<sub>w</sub> = 4 × 5 = 20 W as heat, while storing ½ × 0.4 × 2² = 0.8 J.

beyond: Not for the exam. In power electronics the same laws size the inductor of a buck converter and the output capacitor of a phone charger. At gigahertz frequencies every track on a board acts as a small L and C, so chip designers extract and simulate these parasitics. Search next for inductor saturation, capacitor ESR and parasitic extraction.
